reference.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies / WHO envenoming guidance
clinicalPearls: Loxoscelism ranges from a self-limiting local lesion to a necrotic ulcer, and less commonly a systemic (viscerocutaneous) illness with haemolysis
The bite is often initially painless; over hours a central blister with surrounding pallor and erythema may evolve into a sinking, dusky lesion and eschar
A dependent or gravity-influenced spread of discolouration and the classic red-white-blue appearance suggest developing dermonecrosis
Systemic loxoscelism, more common in children, features fever, malaise and intravascular haemolysis, sometimes with haemoglobinuria and acute kidney injury
Most necrotic wounds attributed to spiders are actually other conditions; confirmed recluse exposure requires the spider to be endemic and ideally identified
Management is largely supportive with wound care, analgesia and monitoring for haemolysis; surgical debridement is deferred until the lesion has fully demarcated
There is no local pain-predominant cramping syndrome as in widow bites, which aids differentiation
reference.pathophysiology: Recluse venom contains sphingomyelinase D (phospholipase D), which acts on cell membranes and endothelium to trigger complement activation, neutrophil recruitment and intravascular thrombosis. This produces localised vascular occlusion and ischaemic dermonecrosis, with a characteristic gravity-dependent spread of injury. In systemic loxoscelism the enzyme induces complement-mediated haemolysis of red cells, releasing free haemoglobin that can precipitate acute kidney injury; disseminated intravascular coagulation may accompany severe cases. The delayed, evolving nature of the lesion reflects progressive microvascular thrombosis rather than direct cytolysis alone.
additionalDifferentials: Bacterial skin and soft-tissue infection or abscess
Cutaneous anthrax or other necrotic infection
Other arthropod bite or chemical/thermal injury
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film for haemolysis
Haptoglobin, lactate dehydrogenase, reticulocytes and bilirubin for intravascular haemolysis
Urinalysis for haemoglobinuria and renal function tests
Coagulation studies if disseminated intravascular coagulation is suspected
Wound assessment over serial reviews to track demarcation
Consideration of infective causes when a necrotic lesion lacks clear envenomation history
redFlags: Systemic features of fever, malaise and dark urine suggesting haemolysis
Falling haemoglobin or evidence of acute kidney injury
Rapidly spreading necrosis or signs of superadded necrotising infection
reference.prognosis: Most bites heal with conservative wound care, though large necrotic ulcers may take weeks to months and can scar. Systemic loxoscelism with haemolysis is uncommon but potentially life-threatening, particularly in children, and requires close monitoring.
pitfalls: Over-diagnosing recluse bites for necrotic wounds outside the spider's endemic range, missing infection or other pathology
Performing early aggressive debridement before the lesion has demarcated, worsening the defect
Failing to screen for and monitor systemic haemolysis, especially in children
Treating a necrotising soft-tissue infection as a benign spider bite
management: Provide supportive wound care with cleansing, immobilisation, elevation and dressings, together with analgesia and tetanus prophylaxis
Defer surgical debridement until the necrotic lesion has fully demarcated to avoid enlarging the wound
Monitor for systemic loxoscelism with serial full blood count, haemolysis markers and urinalysis, particularly in children who are most at risk
Treat intravascular haemolysis with hydration, transfusion as required and management of haemoglobinuria to protect renal function
Manage disseminated intravascular coagulation with supportive haematological measures if it develops
Reserve antibiotics for genuine secondary bacterial infection rather than the necrotic lesion itself, and escalate to critical care for severe systemic envenomation
